payload.problem_addressed: Automated LaTeX manuscript revision pipelines regenerate whole sections to fix a local defect, which lets the PDF still build while unrelated numbers/citations silently drift (non-monotonic revision).
payload.method_summary: PatchWrite replaces whole-slot rewriting with a single bounded-interval EDIT N M (span <=40 lines) inside a refinement loop. A candidate edit is committed as the new HEAD only if it passes a compile gate (scans the pdflatex log for fatal errors rather than trusting any produced PDF) and an evidence gate (every \cite key and numeric token must be attested in a citation registry or experimental log); otherwise HEAD is rolled back unchanged. Illegal/over-long edits fall back to legacy whole-slot rewrite.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper contributes a stricter, empirically validated acceptance predicate (fatal-log compile gate + cite/numeric evidence locks) layered on an existing bounded-edit mechanism (PaperSolver's EDIT N M), an oracle stress protocol (24 manuscripts x 8 faults, 768 jobs) with ablations isolating each gate's contribution, a live-model companion study across two writer models (Qwen3.7-plus, Kimi K2.6) measuring parse/compile/gate/fault-fixed rates for self-proposed edits, and a small human rater comparison plus in-product log analysis.
payload.headline_results: On the oracle stress test, whole-slot rewrite mutates an unrelated 'encoder uses 12 layers' line in 0/192 cases while PatchWrite preserves it in 192/192; disabling the compile gate drops accept rate to 0, disabling the evidence gate lets a hallucinated citation through. With the writer model itself proposing edits, accept rate starts at 75% (limited almost entirely by the model trying to delete lines with an empty replacement, which the grammar rejects) and reaches 100% after a one-line prompt fix telling it to comment out instead of empty a line -- though fault-fixed rate of accepted patches then drops from 93.75% to 84.9%, and every accepted patch still cleared both gates (no hallucinated citation or unattested number).
claimed_advantages: Surgical, bounded edits with a compile-log-scan gate preserve unrelated lab-grounded facts that whole-slot regeneration silently mutates.
Cite/numeric evidence locks catch hallucinated citations and unattested numbers that a compile-only check would miss.
A rollback-on-failure invariant guarantees the file on disk is always the last compiling, evidence-clean manuscript.
limitations: All eight injected faults are scripted rather than adversarially searched.
The edit grammar has no explicit delete verb, causing systematic fallback on faults requiring line deletion.

The evidence gate checks that a cite key or number is attested anywhere, not that it is the correct attested value for the specific claim (documented near-misses: a real-but-wrong citation key, a compiling-but-not-byte-exact numeric fix).
The human rater pool is an exploratory two-rater pool (author + one unpaid rater), not a validated study.
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core mechanism -- gate candidate edits/programs on a machine-checkable acceptance predicate (compile + domain-specific validity checks) and roll back to the last known-good state on failure rather than accepting anything that merely 'looks done' -- is directly analogous to hexgen's frozen verifier gating best-of-N candidate programs (care area 1: structural validity via execution-gated acceptance). The documented failure mode where a model can pass gates with a technically-valid-but-wrong output (attested-but-incorrect citation key, non-identity numeric fix) is a useful cautionary parallel for hexgen's verifier: passing compile + quality-bound checks does not guarantee the *intended* geometric repair, so verifier checks that are locally satisfiable but semantically off-target are a real risk. The bounded-interval edit-and-rollback loop (vs. whole-section/whole-program regeneration) is also a transferable idea for a repair/edit-distillation approach to fixing a hexgen model's own broken rollouts (DAgger-style), since it keeps unrelated, already-correct parts of a candidate program untouched.
payload.reviewer_notes: Domain is LaTeX manuscript revision, not CAD/program synthesis, so this is a methodological analogy rather than a directly reusable component; the 'grammar has no delete verb' failure and the evidence-gate's attested-but-wrong-key failure are the most instructive negative results for us, since they show how a plausible-looking gate can still admit an unintended (though technically valid) edit. Single-author paper, uses proprietary/product logs (Solus) as a secondary evidence source with a stated conflict of interest.

provenance.method_summary: commits only when pdflatex is clean and every \cite key and numeric token is attested in a registry or experimental log, and rolling back to the last compiling HEAD otherwise

payload.problem_addressed: Inference-time pipelines that sample N candidates, filter with a learned safety/proxy model, and return the proxy-feasible output with highest learned reward can systematically select outputs that pass the learned constraint but violate the true safety criterion -- termed 'safety hacking'.
payload.method_summary: The paper formalizes constrained Best-of-N (CBoNN) sampling and derives finite-N bounds on safety-hacking probability governed by the joint upper reward tails of safe vs. unsafe-but-proxy-feasible outputs: if unsafe-but-feasible outputs have the heavier reward tail, safety hacking becomes asymptotically certain as N grows even with small false-positive mass and small average proxy errors. It further shows policies within a bounded chi-squared divergence of the proxy-feasible reference distribution admit an N-independent safety-hacking bound, and instantiates this coverage-control principle as constrained pessimistic sampling, validated on a toy problem and LLM experiments.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper contributes a formal two-stage failure model (safety-proxy contamination of the feasible set, then reward-maximization amplification of that contamination) for constrained Best-of-N inference-time scaling, finite-N and N-independent theoretical bounds on safety-hacking probability, and a coverage-control mitigation (constrained pessimistic sampling) that limits amplification without being able to repair contamination.
payload.headline_results: Toy and LLM experiments confirm that safety hacking probability grows with N when unsafe-but-feasible outputs have heavier reward tails than safe ones, that coverage control (bounded chi-squared divergence / pessimistic sampling) limits this N-driven amplification but cannot eliminate risk from an already-contaminated feasible set, and that regularized selection is not necessarily safer than plain constrained Best-of-N for every reward proxy.
claimed_advantages: Provides a principled diagnosis (reward-tail asymmetry) for why scaling N in filter-then-select inference pipelines can make safety worse rather than better.
Coverage control (bounded chi-squared divergence / pessimistic sampling) provably bounds amplification independent of N.
limitations: Coverage control only limits amplification of an already-contaminated proxy-feasible set; it cannot repair contamination.
Admitted unsafe outputs may still be favored, and regularized (pessimistic) selection is not guaranteed to be safer than unconstrained best-of-N for every reward proxy.
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Directly transferable as a cautionary framework for hexgen's own best-of-N + frozen-verifier design (care area 6): even though hexgen's verifier is machine-checkable (compiles, zero inverted elements, quality bounds, boundary fidelity) rather than a learned safety model, any residual gap between 'passes the verifier' and 'is a genuinely good/valid mesh program' functions as an imperfect proxy, and this paper's result implies that scaling best-of-N could systematically amplify selection of programs that satisfy the verifier's checks by construction/edge-case but are geometrically undesirable if the scoring/ranking signal used to pick among verifier-passing candidates has a heavier tail on such edge cases. Their finite-N and coverage-control (bounded-divergence pessimistic sampling) machinery is a candidate tool for auditing or bounding this risk in hexgen's own best-of-N selection step, and for reasoning about how large N can safely be scaled before verifier-edge-case exploitation becomes likely.
payload.reviewer_notes: The paper's 'safety' framing is about harmful/unsafe LLM outputs, not geometric validity, so the transfer is at the level of the general statistical mechanism (imperfect proxy + best-of-N reward-tail amplification), not a directly reusable method; still relevant since hexgen's verifier, while much stricter than a learned safety classifier, is not infallible (e.g. quality bounds and boundary-fidelity checks are threshold-based approximations) and best-of-N selection among verifier-passing candidates could in principle exploit gaps the same way.

payload.impact_rationale: Offers a concrete, validated pattern (bounded local edit + compile-gate + domain-evidence-gate + rollback-to-last-good) for care area 1 (structural validity), specifically for a repair/edit-distillation loop rather than whole-program regeneration -- directly useful if hexgen ever needs to repair a model's own broken rollouts at sub-program granularity instead of just accept/reject via best-of-N. Impact is capped because the domain (LaTeX text) is far from CAD/DSL programs and the paper's evaluation is small-scale/single-author.
payload.effort_rationale: Reusing the *idea* is cheap, but building an actual bounded-edit grammar over the hex-meshing DSL (atomic edit ops, line/command addressing, a fatal-vs-recoverable failure classifier analogous to the pdflatex log scan) plus wiring it into the existing frozen verifier as a gate is a non-trivial new subsystem, not a drop-in reuse.

payload.impact_rationale: Provides a theoretical lens (reward-tail amplification under an imperfect proxy) that is useful for auditing whether hexgen's best-of-N + frozen-verifier pipeline could be exploiting edge cases in the quality-bound thresholds as N scales, but it's a diagnostic framework rather than a method we would directly adopt, and hexgen's verifier is machine-checkable/near-deterministic rather than a learned safety proxy, weakening direct transfer.
payload.effort_rationale: Applying the coverage-control (bounded-divergence pessimistic sampling) idea would require translating their formalism to hexgen's verifier + candidate-ranking setup and validating empirically that it changes anything given the verifier is already strict, which is moderate exploratory analysis work rather than a straightforward implementation.
